  • Longer episodes contribute more timesteps to the statistics.
  • Validation uses the same training statistics; it does not fit its own.
  • Statistics are fitted before action padding, so repeated padding actions do not affect the fit.
  • A loaded policy reuses saved statistics, even when new demonstrations are supplied.

The Normalizer API covers validation and storage behavior.

items.title: Work through an action chunk
items.text:
Consider an illustrative episode with four aligned rows (s0, a0) through (s3, a3) and a chunk length of three:

Start state Padding enabled Padding disabled s0 [a0, a1, a2] [a0, a1, a2] s1 [a1, a2, a3] [a1, a2, a3] s2 [a2, a3, a3] Omitted. s3 [a3, a3, a3] Omitted.

The final action repeats; the window never borrows actions from the next episode. There is one state input, not a history of three observations. Repeated target actions participate in the loss; there is no padding mask.

For an episode of length T and chunk length H:

  • Padding enabled (the trainer default): T examples.
  • Padding disabled: max(0, T - H + 1) examples.

Each dataset item is a pair of fresh float32 tensors: state (state_dim,), target (H, action_dim). For a batch of 32 with five state features, two action features, and H=8, the shapes are (32, 5) and (32, 8, 2). This is an illustrative batch, not a measured dataset sample.

items.title: Batch without crossing boundaries
items.text:
Per-episode datasets are combined after their windows are constructed. The training loader shuffles examples and drops its last incomplete batch. Validation keeps order and includes its final partial batch.

Consequences:

  • An episode boundary is preserved even when batch members come from different episodes.
  • Fewer training examples than batch_size yields no training batches and an explicit error.
  • Changing padding or chunk length changes the sample count and therefore steps per epoch.
  • Validation loss must weight batch means by example count; see metrics.

Existing boundary and numerical tests are mapped in Tests and checks. Next, follow the training lifecycle.

items.title: Evaluation and metric interpretation
items.text: A lower imitation loss and a stronger rollout score answer different questions. Loss measures agreement with demonstration targets; rollouts measure behavior when the policy's own actions determine subsequent observations.

items.title: Read the four metric streams
items.text:
File, when CSV logging is enabled Meaning Use train.csv loss_window_mean, weighted by examples since the previous report; window_examples_count records its size. Monitor optimization. validation.csv loss_mean over the held-out loader, weighted by examples; examples_count records its size. Monitor demonstration fit. eval.csv mean_reward, episode count, and video paths from selection rollouts. Rank checkpoints and drive plateau stopping. final_eval.csv Final score and budget, selected checkpoint_step, its selection_mean_reward, and stop_reason. Assess the selected policy on separate evaluation streams.

All files use global_step as the optimizer-step coordinate. Training rows also record a zero-based epoch. A loss window can cross epoch boundaries, so its row is not necessarily an epoch average.

W&B uses corresponding train/*, validation/*, eval/*, and final/* namespaces when enabled. The final stop reason is a CSV field and W&B run-summary value, not a numeric final/* metric.

items.title: Weight losses by examples
items.text:
Suppose validation produces a batch of three examples with mean loss 2 and a batch of one with mean loss 6:

correct mean = (3 * 2 + 1 * 6) / 4 = 3
mean of batch means = (2 + 6) / 2 = 4

The implementation uses the first calculation. This matters because validation retains its final partial batch. An empty validation loader raises instead of returning a numerical average.

Validation temporarily uses evaluation mode and disables gradient recording. Dropout is disabled, but flow loss still samples noise and interpolation times. The trainer recreates the validation-loss generator at each pass, making those draws comparable when batch order and shapes stay unchanged. See randomness.

items.title: Follow one rollout
items.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Reset with episode environment seed] --> B[Normalize current state]
    B --> C[Sample normalized action chunk]
    C --> D[Denormalize and clip to bounds]
    D --> E[Execute next action]
    E --> F{Episode ended?}
    F -->|Yes| G[Keep maximum observed reward]
    F -->|No| H{Chunk exhausted?}
    H -->|No| E
    H -->|Yes| B

The evaluator predicts only when the chunk is exhausted. Intermediate observations update the environment state but do not trigger a new prediction. A termination or truncation discards unused actions from that chunk.

Before stepping, it checks the action shape and finiteness, clips to the environment's action bounds, and converts each action to float32. Evaluation uses model.eval() and no gradients, then restores the previous top-level training flag and closes the environment.

items.title: Understand mean_reward
items.text:
For episode i, record its largest observed step reward r_i. The reported score is:

mean_reward = (r_1 + ... + r_N) / N

For two illustrative episodes with rewards [0.1, 0.6, 0.4] and [0.2, 0.8], the score is (0.6 + 0.8) / 2 = 0.7. It is neither cumulative return nor the proportion of successful episodes.

In the locked Gym environment, coverage is block–goal intersection area divided by goal area. Step reward is clip(coverage / 0.95, 0, 1); success termination requires coverage greater than 0.95. Time-limit truncation is a separate way to end a rollout. These details follow executable environment code rather than its simplified reward prose. Environment implementation.

items.title: Separate selection from final assessment
items.text:
Selection evaluations save candidates before checking whether training should stop. Final assessment reloads the best retained candidate; it does not rerank checkpoints.

sequenceDiagram
    participant T as Training driver
    participant E as Evaluator
    participant C as Checkpoint storage
    participant S as Plateau tracker
    loop Each scheduled selection evaluation (also final training step)
        T->>E: Score current policy with selection streams
        E-->>T: Mean of episode maximum rewards
        T->>C: Save and retain best K plus latest
        opt Stopper enabled and training not complete
            T->>S: Update with selection score and global step
            S-->>T: Stop requested?
        end
    end
    Note over T,C: After completion or stop request
    T->>C: Load highest-scoring retained checkpoint
    C-->>T: Selected policy and normalizer
    T->>E: Evaluate with separate final streams
    E-->>T: Final assessment
    Note over T,C: Final score does not change checkpoint ranking
Evaluation Policy Random streams Budget Periodic and final training step Current policy. EVAL_ENV, EVAL_POLICY. eval_episodes. After completion or early stopping Best retained checkpoint. FINAL_EVAL_ENV, FINAL_EVAL_POLICY. final_eval_episodes.

Both budgets default to 100. Selection scores determine retention and plateau stopping; final scores do neither. Reusing a fixed selection setup helps compare checkpoints, but selecting the best result also favors that setup. Separate final streams provide another assessment without changing the selected policy.

items.title: Sweep objective and final assessment
items.text:
The supplied sweep YAMLs name eval/mean_reward as their objective and maximize it. The logger defines a maximum summary for this metric, so the best observed periodic score remains available alongside its history. Periodic evaluations therefore provide both checkpoint-selection evidence and search feedback.

Final evaluation uses separate streams and reports final/mean_reward; the supplied sweep definitions do not optimize that metric. Separate streams do not make the result permanently independent of selection: if you choose configurations or revise the search based on final scores, those scores become part of your selection process. Confirm promising settings across multiple seeds and report that process explicitly.

See Sweep configuration for the inputs and Inspect sweep trials for the outputs.

items.title: Interpret results with the run settings
items.text:
• Compare rollout scores using the same environment, episode budget, random-stream choices, chunk horizon, and flow integration settings.
  • Treat one-episode smoke tests as pipeline checks, not reliable quality estimates.
  • Repeat comparisons across multiple training seeds and report the spread, not only the best run. Keep paired evaluation settings consistent within each comparison; one fixed seed cannot establish robustness to training variability.
  • Do not compare MSE and flow training losses as though their targets were identical.
  • Check both demonstration fit and rollout behavior: errors can move a policy into observations absent from its demonstrations.
  • Videos help explain behavior but do not replace aggregate scores. Only the first configured episodes are recorded; videos are independently controlled and not pruned with checkpoints.

For field contracts, see ExperimentLogger and evaluate_policy. For storage decisions, continue to checkpoints.

For practical steps, see Configure and compare experiments and Inspect results and diagnose a run.

items.title: Push-T: task, demonstrations, and policy inputs
items.text:
Push-T is a planar manipulation task: a circular pusher moves a T-shaped block toward a target pose. The action is the pusher's target (x, y) position, not a force or a displacement. The environment bounds each coordinate to [0, 512]. Environment description.

The implementation in hw1/ learns from demonstrations, then measures behavior in simulated rollouts. It does not update the policy from rollout rewards. For commands, start with the orientation.

items.title: Separate the task from its representations
items.text:
Representation Information given to a policy Used here? State Pusher position, block position, and block angle: five numbers. Yes. Keypoints Positions describing the block's geometry, with pusher position supplied separately in the Gym package. No. Pixels An RGB image; a separate variant also includes pusher position. No.

These are observation choices for the same task, not interchangeable tensor formats. The Gym package calls its keypoint-style option environment_state_agent_pos; image options are pixels and pixels_agent_pos. Supported observations.

The state vector is ordered [pusher_x, pusher_y, block_x, block_y, block_angle]. Positions and action targets use the same simulation coordinate frame, bounded to [0, 512]; these are environment coordinates, not physical meters. The angle is in radians. State/action implementation.

The local evaluator explicitly creates:

gym.make("gym_pusht/PushT-v0", obs_type="state", render_mode="rgb_array")

render_mode="rgb_array" enables frames for optional videos. It does not make images the policy's observations. The locked gym-pusht version is 0.1.6; its registration limits an episode to 300 steps. Upstream registration.

items.title: Where the demonstrations come from
items.text:
The downloader uses the simulation archive distributed with Diffusion Policy. That project documents pusht.zip and the Zarr replay layout; gym-pusht is an adaptation of its environment. These provenance links do not mean this repository implements Diffusion Policy's diffusion model. Training-data distribution, environment acknowledgement.

The upstream collection script records mouse-controlled demonstrations, pairing the current state with the commanded action and also recording images and keypoints. This explains the multiple fields in the replay store; the downloaded artifact was not inspected or recollected while writing this guide. Collection source.

items.title: Which artifact and fields this code consumes
items.text:
Item Local contract Download URL https://diffusion-policy.cs.columbia.edu/data/training/pusht.zip Extracted path <data-dir>/pusht/pusht_cchi_v7_replay.zarr data/state Expected (N, 5) state rows, converted to float32. data/action Expected (N, 2) action rows, converted to float32. meta/episode_ends Expected (E,) exclusive episode-end offsets, converted to int64.

The loader reads only these three arrays. Other archive fields, such as images or keypoints, are not model inputs. ZIP is the distribution container; Zarr is the array store inside it. A repackaged dataset with the same task name is not automatically compatible with these paths or semantics. Upstream replay layout.

Here N is the number of recorded timesteps and E the number of episodes; these symbols do not assert measured counts. These shapes describe the expected state-based artifact interface. The code derives feature dimensions from loaded data rather than enforcing five/two features or a fixed demonstration count. Do not treat comments containing counts as validation of a local dataset. The data pipeline explains episode and shape checks.

items.title: Keep compatibility questions separate
items.text:
The v7 in pusht_cchi_v7_replay.zarr identifies this replay artifact; it does not identify every dataset or environment called Push-T.

What changes? What to verify before comparing or reusing it Dataset release The demonstrations themselves, including trajectory contents and episode membership, may differ. Packaging conversion Container or field names may change; verify state/action ordering, coordinate scales, alignment, and exclusive episode offsets rather than assuming a format conversion preserves them. Observation representation State, keypoints, and images require different model inputs, even if recorded from the same trajectories. Environment or evaluation setup Version, reset distribution, time limit, reward definition, and action execution horizon can affect scores independently of the dataset.

For this implementation, compatibility means matching the consumed fields and their semantics and evaluating with the intended environment settings. ZIP-versus-Zarr alone says nothing about those contracts.

items.title: Two policy families, one interface
items.text:
Both policies take one normalized state and return a normalized action chunk shaped (batch, chunk_size, action_dim).

Policy Training target Inference mse Demonstrated action chunk; minimize mean squared error. Predict the chunk directly. flow Velocity from Gaussian noise toward the demonstrated chunk, at a sampled interpolation time. Integrate the learned velocity field from fresh Gaussian noise using forward Euler steps.

The default fresh model is MSE with an eight-action chunk. Flow sampling defaults to ten integration steps. Both use the same demonstration pipeline and rollout evaluator; their loss values describe different objectives and should not be compared as a shared quality score.

Continue with demonstrations to batches, evaluation, or the policy reference.

For implementation changes, follow Change or add a policy.

items.title: Random streams and reproducibility
items.text: The trainer gives each stochastic responsibility its own identity. Changing how often validation runs should not consume the random draws used by training loss. This separation is implemented by RandomStreamFactory, not by repeatedly setting a global seed.

items.title: An identity has four coordinates
items.text:
Coordinate Role Example Root seed Identifies the experiment family. --seed 42. Stream ID Names a permanent responsibility. TRAIN_LOSS. Variation Selects another realization of that responsibility. --train-loss-variation 1. Index Identifies a peer within the stream. Rollout episode 3.

The implementation passes [stream ID, variation, index, root seed] to NumPy SeedSequence, keeping the field order and explicit zero index stable. NumPy generators use PCG64; Torch generators receive a derived unsigned 64-bit seed.

The factory stores no advancing generator state. Every request creates a fresh generator at its starting position. Keep a generator object to advance through draws; request the same identity again to replay from the beginning.

items.title: See replay versus advancement
items.text:
This illustrative snippet draws numbers only; it does not train or evaluate a policy:

from hw1_imitation.randomness import RandomStreamFactory, StreamId

streams = RandomStreamFactory(root_seed=42)
a = streams.numpy(StreamId.TRAIN_LOSS, variation=0)
first = a.normal(size=3)
second = a.normal(size=3)  # Continues the same generator.

b = streams.numpy(StreamId.TRAIN_LOSS, variation=0)
replayed_first = b.normal(size=3)  # Replays first, not second.
c = streams.numpy(StreamId.TRAIN_LOSS, variation=1)  # Another realization.

Creating a again before every batch would restart its noise sequence. The trainer deliberately retains the training-loss generator instead.

items.title: Know each stream's lifetime
items.text:
Responsibility Permanent ID Lifetime in the trainer Episode split DATA_SPLIT = 1 Created for the train/validation split. Fresh model initialization MODEL_INIT = 2 CPU generator used while building the model. Training loader TRAIN_LOADER = 3 Attached to the loader; advances across iterations. Validation loader VALIDATION_LOADER = 4 Attached to the ordered loader; retained across passes. Training loss TRAIN_LOSS = 5 One generator advances across batches and epochs, including noise, times, and active dropout. Validation loss VALIDATION_LOSS = 6 Recreated for each complete validation pass; reused within that pass. Selection environment and policy EVAL_ENV = 7, EVAL_POLICY = 8 Fresh identity per episode index on every selection call. Final environment and policy FINAL_EVAL_ENV = 9, FINAL_EVAL_POLICY = 10 Separate identities per episode in the final call.

An ordered validation loader still has its own generator for loader internals. It is distinct from the generator passed to the stochastic validation loss.

During a rollout, the policy generator advances across chunks in that episode. The next episode uses its own index. A longer earlier episode therefore does not consume the next episode's policy draws. Each evaluation call starts episode indexing at zero; periodic calls reuse matching identities.

items.title: Vary one source deliberately
items.text:
With the root seed fixed, changing eval_env_variation changes selection-environment seeds while leaving training-loss and model-initialization identities unchanged. Changing eval_policy_variation changes policy sampling streams instead.

Keep this distinction when interpreting a comparison:

  • MSE inference in evaluation mode is deterministic for fixed inputs and weights, so a policy-sampling variation may have no effect.
  • Flow inference consumes noise, even in evaluation mode.
  • Active dropout consumes the supplied generator during training; eval() disables dropout draws.
  • Changing an algorithm's draw order or tensor shapes can change its results despite an unchanged identity.

items.title: What reproducibility does and does not promise
items.text:
Stable contract Boundary A repeated identity derives the same starting seed under unchanged derivation behavior. Distinct identities are not mathematically guaranteed never to collide. Factory calls do not mutate global NumPy or Torch RNG state. Other code can still use global RNGs; use the explicit-generator paths consistently. Training and monitoring have separate generators. Library versions, device backends, operations, and sampling shapes can affect numerical replay. Stream IDs are explicitly assigned. Reordering ID declarations is harmless; renumbering or reusing an ID changes established identities.

Match a Torch generator's device to the operation that consumes it. The device does not change the derived integer seed, but CPU and accelerator draws need not be identical.

Root seeds must be nonnegative Python integers. Variations and indices must be Python integers in [0, 2**32); booleans are rejected. An index does not increment automatically.

Policy checkpoints do not store generator states. Loading weights therefore cannot resume an interrupted random trajectory. See checkpoint limits and the RandomStreamFactory API.

To introduce another independent responsibility, follow Add a random stream.

items.title: The training lifecycle
items.text: run_training in train.py coordinates data, optimization, monitoring, and checkpoint selection. It creates experiment outputs rather than returning a trained model. Start with the small-run guide for a runnable command and its side effects.

items.title: Before the first optimizer step
items.text:
1. Parse and validate TrainConfig; create the root random-stream factory.
  2. Select an available PyTorch accelerator or CPU, load demonstrations, and split episodes.
  3. Build a fresh policy and fit normalization, or reconstruct both from --init-from.
  4. Apply an explicit dropout override if supplied; build training and validation loaders using the actual model horizon.
  5. Create a fresh AdamW optimizer, zero the training counter, and create a new experiment directory.
  6. Open checkpoint storage and logging; print the effective configuration summary by default, then create the training progress bar immediately before the training loop.

The run directory is hw1/exp/seed_<seed>_<timestamp>[_suffix]/ when launched from hw1/; --exp-name adds the suffix. Disabling metric outputs does not prevent directory creation.

items.title: One optimizer step, several possible checks
items.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Training batch] --> B[Compute loss and update AdamW]
    B --> C[Increment global step]
    C --> D{Logging due?}
    D -->|Yes| E[Report loss window]
    D -->|No| F{Validation due?}
    E --> F
    F -->|Yes| G[Measure held-out loss]
    F -->|No| H{Rollout evaluation due?}
    G --> H
    H -->|Yes| I[Score policy and save checkpoint]
    I --> N{Stopper enabled and training incomplete?}
    N -->|Yes| J[Check plateau stopping]
    N -->|No| K
    H -->|No| K{Complete or stop requested?}
    J --> K
    K -->|No| A
    K -->|Yes| L[Evaluate best retained checkpoint]
    L --> M[Close outputs and clean temporary checkpoints]

Each training step calls model.train(), clears gradients, computes the policy's scalar loss, backpropagates, and updates AdamW. Both MSE and flow use demonstrated action chunks; flow also samples noise and interpolation times. Dropout draws from the explicit training-loss generator when enabled.

items.title: Understand the scheduling units
items.text:
Setting Default Trigger num_epochs 400 Full passes through the training loader. log_interval 100 Optimizer steps between training-loss reports. validation_interval 100 Optimizer steps between validation passes. eval_interval 10,000 Optimizer steps between selection rollouts. eval_episodes 100 Episodes in each selection evaluation. final_eval_episodes 100 Episodes in the separate final evaluation.

Logging, validation, and selection evaluation also run at the final training step, even when it is not an interval boundary. Loss windows can span epochs. Early stopping happens at a selection evaluation and can end the run between the other intervals; pending training-loss totals are flushed at shutdown.

For example, with 12 batches per epoch and two epochs, there are 24 optimizer steps. If all intervals exceed 24, monitoring still runs at step 24. Changing batch size changes this step count and how epoch-based warm-up relates to step-based evaluation.

items.title: Early stopping and final evaluation
items.text:
Plateau stopping is disabled unless early_stopping_patience is set. When enabled:

  • Selection rollout reward is the objective to maximize.
  • A gain must be strictly greater than early_stopping_min_delta to reset patience.
  • Warm-up uses early_stopping_min_epochs * steps_per_epoch; stale evaluations count only after that step boundary.
  • Warm-up scores can establish the reference reward. Patience counts evaluation events, not epochs.

After completion or a stop request, the trainer selects the highest-scoring retained checkpoint, breaking ties toward the later step. It loads that policy and runs a final evaluation with separate random streams. Final scores do not change checkpoint ranking. With latest-only retention, the final candidate is normally the latest checkpoint; see retention details.

items.title: Outputs and failure boundaries
items.text:
Output Behavior CSV metrics Separate training, validation, selection, and final-evaluation files when enabled. W&B Metrics, videos, and checkpoint artifacts when enabled; offline mode is rejected. Policy checkpoints Persistent by default; temporary with --save-checkpoints False. Videos Controlled independently by --num-video-episodes; not covered by checkpoint retention.

Temporary checkpoint storage is removed after normal completion and retained if the training body raises. Serialization, device, data, and upload failures can stop the run; cleanup failures have their own behavior described in checkpoints.

See metric interpretation, random-stream lifetimes, and the configuration reference.

items.title: Add or change a random stream
items.text:
Use this guide when a new stochastic responsibility must stay independent of existing draws. If you only need another realization or another episode, use a variation or index instead. Read stream identities and lifetimes first.

This is a procedure for a future code change. The documentation does not introduce a new stream. Source paths below are relative to hw1/src/hw1_imitation/; run checks from hw1/ after setup.

items.title: 1. Choose the right coordinate
items.text:
Need Use Example An independent stochastic responsibility New StreamId. A new operation whose draw count should not affect training-loss noise. Another realization of an existing responsibility Existing stream with another variation. Another train/validation split. A stable peer within one responsibility Existing stream with an explicit index. Evaluation episode number. Another experiment family Another root seed. Repeating an entire experiment.

Do not allocate a new ID for every seed or episode. Do not reuse a training generator merely because it is already in scope.

items.title: 2. Allocate a permanent ID
items.text:
In randomness.py, inspect the registry before editing. It currently assigns IDs 1–10 and marks 11 as the next candidate.

  1. Choose a descriptive responsibility name and an unused explicit integer.
  2. Preserve every existing ID, including when renaming a member.
  3. Never reuse a retired ID. Update the next-ID comment if applicable.
  4. Preserve the identity encoding order [stream, variation, index, root_seed], including the explicit zero index.

An illustrative future responsibility could use NEW_RESPONSIBILITY = 11 only if 11 is still unused when the change is made. That symbol does not exist today.

items.title: 3. Route configuration to the consumer
items.text:
If users need to select realizations:

  1. Add a named variation field with default zero to TrainConfig in train.py.
  2. Validate it through RandomStreamFactory.validate with the new stream, rejecting invalid values before expensive work where possible.
  3. Pass the field explicitly to the consumer; verify the dataclass-derived CLI flag and configuration reporting.

The factory accepts Python integer variations and indices in [0, 2**32), excluding booleans. Current TrainConfig explicitly validates its listed stream variations, while final-evaluation variations are validated when used. Do not assume a newly added field is automatically checked by the existing validation loop.

Use .torch(..., device=...), .numpy(...), or .seed(...) according to the consumer. Match a Torch generator to the sampling device. Avoid global manual_seed, global NumPy draws, or hidden default generators in the new path.

items.title: 4. Decide where the generator lives
items.text:
Desired behavior Creation point Advance across batches/epochs Create once outside the loop and retain the object. Replay draws for each complete assessment Recreate with the same identity at the start of the assessment; retain within it. Isolate peers from each other's draw counts Create from a stable explicit index for each peer.

Follow existing patterns: training loss advances through a run, validation loss restarts per pass, and each rollout episode has separate environment/policy identities. The factory does not advance indices automatically.

Pass the generator through every stochastic helper, including active dropout. If a nested module needs explicit RNG routing, inspect rng_modules.py rather than assuming ordinary nn.Sequential forwards a generator keyword.

items.title: 5. Verify isolation and integration
items.text:
Existing checks, run from hw1/:

uv run --no-sync pytest \
  tests/test_randomness.py tests/test_evaluation_streams.py \
  tests/test_rng_modules.py tests/test_dropout_integration.py -v

Expected result: existing identity, replay, default-RNG isolation, and monitoring-isolation checks still pass. Then run the complete CI checks.

For the new path, review whether the change demonstrates each contract below. Existing tests may not exercise a newly introduced responsibility; update relevant tests or propose additional coverage within the agreed scope of that implementation task.

  • Same identity and compatible backend replay the initial draws.
  • Reusing one generator advances it; unrelated draws do not advance it.
  • Changing a variation changes only the intended responsibility's identity.
  • Stable peer indices survive unrelated peers consuming more draws.
  • Invalid coordinates fail, and generator/device mismatches are not hidden.
  • Existing permanent seed identities remain unchanged.

items.title: Common mistakes
items.text:
• Recreating a training generator in every batch unintentionally repeats its noise.
  • Changing stream numbers to match declaration order breaks established identities.
  • Using loop position as an index after reordering peers changes their identities.
  • A passing replay test alone does not prove isolation from global RNG state.
  • A fixed seed does not promise identical results across devices or changed sampling operations.

See RandomStreamFactory for the current API.

items.title: Change the checkpoint format
items.text:
Use this guide when a policy change requires new serialized state or different interpretation of existing fields. Start by reading the current checkpoint contract and identifying which consumers would be affected.

This page describes how to plan and verify a future implementation. The current format remains version 1, and the current loader rejects unsupported versions. There is no automatic migration path implemented here.

Source paths below are relative to hw1/src/hw1_imitation/. Run existing checks from hw1/ with the development environment.

items.title: 1. Define the contract change
items.text:
Record the old and proposed meaning, not just a new dictionary key:

Question Why it matters Is this architecture, learned state, normalization, runtime training configuration, or inference configuration? Determines reconstruction and which component owns the field. Is a missing value safe to default? A silent default can change behavior without an obvious load failure. Can old weights and normalizers still represent the model? Shape compatibility alone does not establish semantic compatibility. Does the proposal add optimizer/RNG/training position? That changes the policy-only contract and needs an explicit resumption design. Which files must remain loadable? Establishes the compatibility target before implementation.

Trace save_policy, load_policy, PolicyConfig, policy construction, dropout restoration, and the trainer's --init-from path. Check direct inference users as well as training.

items.title: 2. Choose a version and compatibility policy
items.text:
For an incompatible interpretation or required new content, plan a version bump rather than silently reinterpreting version 1.

Proposed policy Implementation responsibility Reject older versions explicitly. Keep a clear unsupported-version error and document the boundary. Support selected older versions. Add an explicit conversion/reader path, validate converted state, and define supported source versions. Export a separate conversion tool. Preserve original files and specify the new output format and verification.

These are design alternatives, not current loader capabilities. Agree on one before implementing it. Do not claim compatibility solely because a version field was changed, and do not weaken weights_only=True to accept legacy whole-model pickle files.

items.title: 3. Update writer and reader together
items.text:
1. Change the schema constant and payload assembly in checkpoint.py according to the chosen policy.
  2. Make the loader validate the new value's type, bounds, dimensions, and relationships before applying it where possible.
  3. Reconstruct architecture and strictly load weights; preserve matching dropout-layer requirements or explicitly migrate their names.
  4. Preserve CPU serialization, normalization copies, inference defaults, requested-device placement, and evaluation mode unless a deliberate contract change says otherwise.
  5. Trace the trainer: loaded architecture and normalization currently win over fresh-model flags, while new-run optimization/evaluation settings come from the invocation.

Keep the atomic write sequence: serialize to a sibling temporary file, replace the destination after success, and clean up. It still does not support concurrent writers to the same destination or guarantee crash durability.

items.title: 4. Review the compatibility matrix
items.text:
Use the matrix as acceptance criteria for the implementation task. Existing tests cover several current-format cases; they do not automatically prove a proposed format works. Update relevant tests, and agree on any additional coverage required by that task.

Case Required outcome New writer → new reader Equivalent architecture, normalized/raw predictions, and inference settings. Existing version 1 file → new reader Explicitly agreed migration or clear rejection. New file → old reader Unsupported-version rejection when the version changes. Missing/malformed required field Actionable failure, without partially publishing a checkpoint. Incompatible weights/statistics/dropout names Rejection unless a deliberate, validated conversion handles it. Failed serialization over an existing file Preserve the old destination. Loaded model used for inference Correct device, evaluation mode, and caller-owned RNG. Loaded model used for further training Fresh optimizer/counters/RNG, unless a separately designed contract changes this.

Compare raw-space predictions as well as weights: an altered normalizer can change behavior with identical parameters. For stochastic policies, use matching generator identities and sampling settings during comparison.

items.title: 5. Run the existing checks
items.text:
uv run --no-sync pytest \
  tests/test_checkpoint.py tests/test_checkpoint_atomicity.py \
  tests/test_checkpoint_retention.py tests/test_checkpoint_retention_properties.py \
  tests/test_dropout_integration.py -v

Expect current serialization, restoration, atomicity, and retention behavior to remain valid or to be intentionally updated for the agreed contract. Then run the full CI sequence.

Finally, update the schema documentation, load examples, and compatibility statement alongside the implementation. Preserve fixture provenance; generating both “old” and “new” files through the new writer does not test backward compatibility.

items.title: Common mistakes
items.text:
• Adding a required field without deciding how existing files fail or migrate.
  • Calling an initialization-from-weights workflow exact training resumption.
  • Assuming serialization success proves behavioral equivalence.
  • Renaming modules without considering weight keys and serialized dropout names.
  • Treating retention metadata or W&B aliases as the policy schema itself.

For today's behavior and commands, use Save, load, and train further.

items.title: Add or change a policy
items.text:
Use this guide when changing policy architecture, loss, or sampling behavior. It describes a future implementation task; the supported policy types remain mse and flow.

Read the policy reference, data pipeline, and randomness guide first. Source paths below are relative to hw1/src/hw1_imitation/; run checks from hw1/ after setup.

items.title: 1. Preserve the public tensor contract
items.text:
Both policy families implement BasePolicy and own an MLP. The diagram shows the extension boundary; the table below specifies the tensor contract.

classDiagram
    class BasePolicy {
        <<abstract>>
        reset_parameters(generator)
        compute_loss(state, action_chunk, generator)
        sample_actions(state, generator, num_steps)
    }
    class PolicyConfig
    class MSEPolicy
    class FlowMatchingPolicy
    class MLP
    BasePolicy <|-- MSEPolicy
    BasePolicy <|-- FlowMatchingPolicy
    BasePolicy --> PolicyConfig : retains config
    MSEPolicy *-- MLP : model
    FlowMatchingPolicy *-- MLP : model
    note for BasePolicy "Caller owns normalization, device, and train/eval mode. No forward implementation."

Method labels omit defaults and keyword-only markers; use the policy reference for complete signatures.

Method Inputs Required behavior reset_parameters(generator) Caller-owned initialization generator. Initialize all parameters through that generator; work with the builder's CPU allocation path. compute_loss(state, action_chunk, generator=...) State (B, S) and target actions (B, H, A), in normalized coordinates. Return a differentiable scalar batch-mean loss. sample_actions(state, generator=..., num_steps=...) State (B, S) and caller-owned sampling generator. Return normalized action chunks (B, H, A).

B is batch size, S state dimension, H chunk size, and A action dimension. The base class exposes these dimensions through PolicyConfig.

Normalization and denormalization belong to the caller. The evaluator validates action chunks, clips them to environment bounds, and executes a chunk before requesting another. Do not embed a second normalization step or change the action meaning without coordinating the whole pipeline.

Loss reduction is part of the contract: the logger and validator weight batch means by example counts. Returning a sum would silently distort those metrics.

items.title: 2. Trace construction and configuration
items.text:
For a new family in model.py:

  1. Implement the BasePolicy methods and validate the architecture it accepts.
  2. Add its name to PolicyType and dispatch it in construct_policy.
  3. Decide whether PolicyConfig needs new architectural fields. That configuration is serialized; coordinate any compatibility change with checkpoint-format work.
  4. Verify build_policy, CLI selection, and checkpoint loading all reach the new constructor.

build_policy constructs on the meta device, allocates empty CPU storage, calls reset_parameters with a supplied CPU generator, then moves the model to the target device. Avoid constructor logic that requires materialized tensors or reads uninitialized parameter values.

Direct construct_policy uses ordinary layer construction and does not promise global-RNG isolation. Preserve the explicit-generator builder and the loader's meta-device reconstruction paths.

items.title: 3. Route randomness and respect mode
items.text:
• Use the supplied generator for stochastic loss sampling, action sampling, and active dropout.
  • If introducing an independent responsibility outside the policy's existing loss/sampling streams, follow Add a random stream.
  • Keep generator and sampling tensor devices compatible.
  • Ensure train() and eval() correctly enable/disable dropout through nested modules.
  • Do not assume every sampler disables gradients. The existing MSE sampler does not; callers use torch.no_grad() for inference.

Existing explicit-RNG layers live in rng_modules.py. Their module names identify serialized dropout probabilities. Ordinary PyTorch dropout is not included in that configuration helper; swapping layer types can change both RNG routing and checkpoint behavior.

items.title: 4. Check trainer and evaluator integration
items.text:
Integration point What to verify Fresh model Requested architecture reaches build_policy; summary reports the effective model. Training step Scalar loss supports backward/optimizer updates and leaves targets unchanged. Validation Evaluation mode and example-weighted aggregation remain correct; stochastic loss uses its own generator. Sampling Output has the configured horizon and action dimensions, with finite values after denormalization. Rollouts Current sample_actions arguments remain supported; an MSE-like policy may ignore num_steps. Checkpoint load Configuration reconstructs the family; strict weights and dropout names match; model returns in evaluation mode. Further training Loaded architecture/horizon win over fresh-model CLI settings; optimizer and counters start fresh.

If a new method needs a different inference control, carry it deliberately through configuration, saving/loading, and evaluation rather than overloading an existing field's meaning.

items.title: 5. Verify behavior, not just shapes
items.text:
Run relevant existing suites:

uv run --no-sync pytest \
  tests/test_checkpoint.py tests/test_numerical_correctness.py \
  tests/test_randomness.py tests/test_dropout_integration.py \
  tests/test_evaluation_budgets.py -v

Current parameterizations cover the existing families. Passing them alone does not exercise a new family. Update relevant cases for an authorized policy change and agree on any additional coverage beyond that task's scope.

Review these acceptance checks:

  1. Initialization is reproducible and leaves default RNG state unchanged.
  2. Loss and gradients behave correctly on a small synthetic batch.
  3. Sampling returns normalized (B, H, A) values and consumes only intended RNG draws.
  4. Evaluation mode changes only intended behavior, such as disabling dropout.
  5. Saving/loading preserves raw-space predictions under matching inference settings.
  6. Fresh and checkpoint-initialized trainer paths use the actual architecture consistently.

Use the full CI checks after focused checks. A real-data training run is a separate integration step; tests with synthetic data do not establish policy quality.

items.title: Common mistakes
items.text:
• Adding a class but omitting the type literal or construction dispatch.
  • Returning flattened actions where the evaluator expects an action chunk.
  • Applying normalization twice or changing coordinate units silently.
  • Using global noise or ordinary dropout that bypasses explicit generators.
  • Reusing old checkpoint keys after changing their semantics without a compatibility decision.
  • Comparing a new loss scale directly with another family's loss instead of comparing rollout behavior.

items.title: Compare experiments fairly
items.text:
Use this guide when deciding whether a policy or training-setting change improves Push-T behavior. First complete setup and a small local run. Run commands from hw1/.

The commands below launch real training, may download demonstrations, and create outputs. They were checked against the CLI and source, not executed to produce benchmark results for this guide.

items.title: 1. Define the comparison before launching
items.text:
Use individual commands for a planned comparison with chosen settings. Use a hyperparameter sweep to explore a search space through W&B. Both use the same trainer and argument syntax. After a search, confirm promising configurations across several seeds with matched evaluation budgets; a sweep's best trial alone does not establish a robust improvement.

Write down the changed factor and the settings held constant:

Record Why it matters Code revision, environment, dataset path/content Different inputs or implementations can change results. Policy, hidden widths, chunk size, dropout Defines the prediction problem and model. Epochs, batch size, learning rate, weight decay Defines optimization and update count. Root seed and stream variations Controls split, initialization, training noise, and evaluation. Selection/final episode budgets and intervals Controls score variability and selection opportunities. Retention and early stopping Determines which checkpoint reaches final evaluation and how long training runs. Flow integration steps Changes flow inference cost and potentially quality.

Keep matching seeds across alternatives, then repeat the comparison across several root seeds. Report the spread as well as the average. Matching seed numbers does not give different architectures identical weights or identical random draw consumption.

items.title: 2. Name runs and retain evidence
items.text:
For example, compare MSE with dropout disabled versus probability 0.2:

uv run --no-sync src/hw1_imitation/train.py \
  --policy-type mse --dropout-p 0 --seed 42 \
  --num-epochs 20 --batch-size 128 --lr 0.0003 \
  --eval-episodes 5 --final-eval-episodes 100 \
  --checkpoint-top-k 3 --num-video-episodes 0 --log-wandb False \
  --exp-name mse-dropout0

uv run --no-sync src/hw1_imitation/train.py \
  --policy-type mse --dropout-p 0.2 --seed 42 \
  --num-epochs 20 --batch-size 128 --lr 0.0003 \
  --eval-episodes 5 --final-eval-episodes 100 \
  --checkpoint-top-k 3 --num-video-episodes 0 --log-wandb False \
  --exp-name mse-dropout02

These are illustrative budgets, not tuned recommendations. Both retain the current defaults for unspecified settings, including evaluation intervals and disabled early stopping. Repeat both with the same additional seeds, such as 43 and 44.

--exp-name appends a suffix; it does not replace the complete directory name. Expect separate exp/seed_<seed>_<timestamp>_<suffix>/ directories, metric CSVs, and retained checkpoints. W&B and videos are disabled here; CSV logging and persistent checkpoints remain enabled.

Save the exact invocation and code revision with your experiment notes. Local CSVs and policy checkpoints do not capture the complete invocation. W&B records configuration when enabled, but a local-only run should not depend on that service for its records.

items.title: 3. Change policy or randomness deliberately
items.text:
• MSE versus flow: change --policy-type flow and explicitly record --flow-num-steps. Keep the dataset/split and evaluation settings paired; compare rollout scores, not their different loss objectives.
  • A different split: change --data-split-variation while keeping the root seed fixed. This changes train/validation episode membership.
  • A different rollout setup: change --eval-env-variation or --eval-policy-variation independently. Final counterparts are --final-eval-env-variation and --final-eval-policy-variation.
  • Training variability: vary the root seed across repeated runs; changing a root seed affects all derived identities, not only initialization.

See random-stream identities before selecting variations. MSE inference in evaluation mode does not consume policy-sampling noise, so changing that stream alone may not change its result.

For a plateau-stopping experiment, set an explicit policy such as --early-stopping-patience 5 --early-stopping-min-epochs 10 --early-stopping-min-delta 0.005 on each compared run. These are illustrative values. Patience counts stale selection evaluations after warm-up, so also record --eval-interval; equal epoch budgets no longer imply equal work. See the training lifecycle for the strict improvement and warm-up rules.

Dropout accepts 0 <= p < 1; explicit probabilities apply to hidden activations. With fresh models, omission means zero. With loaded models, omission inherits saved per-layer probabilities; see checkpoint initialization.

items.title: 4. Compare the selected policies
items.text:
1. Inspect final_eval.csv for the final score, episode count, selected checkpoint_step, and selection score.
  2. Trace that step in eval.csv; inspect training and validation histories for context.
  3. Check that budgets, stream settings, and retention policies match your comparison plan.
  4. Aggregate across seeds, preserving individual results and failures rather than reporting only the best run.

Smaller selection budgets make checkpoint choice noisier even when the final budget is large. K=0 normally evaluates latest rather than the historical best. Repeatedly changing settings based on final scores also makes those scores part of your selection process; describe that honestly.

items.title: Verify and avoid misleading conclusions
items.text:
Check Mistake it prevents Every run completed final evaluation. Comparing a partial run with a completed run. Compare mean_reward under matching scoring rules. Treating it as cumulative return or success rate. Match update counts when batch size or padding changes. Assuming equal epochs always mean equal optimization work. Inspect warnings and selected checkpoint identity. Assuming retention cleanup or checkpoint selection always succeeded. Report multiple seeds and their variability. Interpreting a single favorable rollout as a robust improvement.

Continue with Inspect results and metric definitions.

items.title: Inspect a run's results
items.text: Use this sequence after a training run completes or fails. You need its experiment directory and the invocation used to create it. Work from hw1/; the default directory is exp/seed_<seed>_<timestamp>[_suffix]/.
path: Inspect results and diagnose a run

items.title: 1. Establish whether the run completed
items.text:
Check the terminal output and process status first. A normal run performs final evaluation before the interactive progress display ends at Done (or Stopped (plateau) for early stopping).

  • A traceback or nonzero exit means the run failed, even if CSV rows or checkpoints exist.
  • Non-interactive output may suppress progress bars.
  • A final CSV row records completed evaluation, but subsequent W&B reporting or cleanup can still fail.
  • Read cleanup warnings before assuming disk contents match the retention limit.

If CSV logging was disabled, there may be no metric files. The output controls explain which files to expect.
path: Inspect results and diagnose a run

items.title: 2. Read metrics in diagnostic order
items.text:
Order File Inspect 1 final_eval.csv Final mean_reward, num_episodes, checkpoint_step, selection_mean_reward, and stop_reason. 2 eval.csv Selection-score history and video_paths; locate the selected step. 3 validation.csv Held-out loss_mean and examples_count. 4 train.csv loss_window_mean, window_examples_count, and progress through optimizer steps.

Each file uses global_step. Training epoch is zero-based; a reporting window can cross epochs. Do not average rows blindly when their example counts differ.

To inspect existing files without modifying them, replace the example directory below and run:

uv run --no-sync python - <<'PY'
import csv
from pathlib import Path

run_dir = Path("exp/REPLACE_WITH_RUN_DIRECTORY")
if not run_dir.is_dir():
    raise SystemExit(f"Run directory not found: {run_dir}")
for name in ("final_eval.csv", "eval.csv", "validation.csv", "train.csv"):
    path = run_dir / name
    if not path.exists():
        print(f"{name}: absent")
        continue
    with path.open(newline="") as stream:
        rows = list(csv.DictReader(stream))
    print(f"{name}: {len(rows)} rows; last={rows[-1] if rows else None}")
PY

Expected output is a row count and last row for each present CSV, or an explicit absence message. This reads the entire CSV into memory and is intended for ordinary local run logs. It does not compute a new evaluation score.
path: Inspect results and diagnose a run

items.title: 3. Locate the policy that was assessed
items.text:
With persistent checkpoints enabled, use the checkpoint_step from final_eval.csv to find:

exp/<run>/checkpoints/policy_step_<checkpoint_step>.pt

The highest numbered checkpoint is latest, not necessarily best. Default retention keeps the best three plus latest; ties favor later steps. Cleanup failures can leave additional files.

With --save-checkpoints False, successful runs remove their temporary checkpoint directory. A metric row can therefore legitimately refer to a checkpoint that no longer exists. Failed runs may retain temporary checkpoints; the temporary prefix contains the run name.

For an available policy file, follow Save, load, and train further. See retention behavior before treating an untracked or leftover file as a selected checkpoint.
path: Inspect results and diagnose a run

items.title: 4. Use videos to explain behavior
items.text:
Selection videos live under videos/step_<step padded to 8 digits>/. Final-evaluation videos live under videos/best_step_<step padded to 8 digits>/. Individual filenames use episode_<index padded to 7 digits>.mp4.

  • The video_paths cell in eval.csv is a JSON list of paths relative to the run directory. Use a JSON parser rather than splitting it on commas.
  • final_eval.csv does not list final video paths; use its selected step and the directory layout.
  • Only the first num_video_episodes episodes are recorded, bounded by the actual evaluation budget.
  • Videos and W&B caches are not removed by policy-checkpoint retention.

Inspect a few rollouts for missed contacts, unstable motion, and whether action chunks carry the pusher past useful states. Treat these as diagnostic observations; the aggregate score still comes from all evaluated episodes.
path: Inspect results and diagnose a run

items.title: Inspect sweep trials
items.text:
Open the sweep URL returned at registration and inspect each trial's status and configuration. The periodic eval/mean_reward history shows checkpoint-selection scores; its maximum summary records the strongest observed score. The supplied YAMLs name this metric as the search objective.

final/mean_reward describes a separate evaluation of the selected checkpoint. It is not the configured sweep objective. Check final/checkpoint_step and final/selection_mean_reward to connect that assessment to selection history. An objective value can be logged before training finishes, so check completion and final metrics before comparing trials.

For local evidence, follow the CSV and checkpoint steps above for each trial's experiment directory. Keep the sweep ID, code revision, and sampled configuration with your comparison. Changing settings based on final scores makes those scores part of the selection process; see metric interpretation.
path: Inspect results and diagnose a run

items.title: 5. Explain surprising results
items.text:
Observation What to check next Training loss improves but rollouts do not. Validation trend, normalization, action semantics, and behavior after the policy leaves demonstration states. Final score differs from selection score. Separate evaluation streams and budgets; it is not a rerun of identical episodes. A file is absent. Logging/video flags, temporary storage, failure point, and whether cleanup already ran. Best score seems missing from final assessment. Retention K, selected step, cleanup warnings, and whether the run completed. Two runs disagree. Exact settings, dataset, code revision, and variation across training seeds.

Use metric interpretation to avoid reading mean_reward as success rate or cumulative return. Before declaring an improvement, follow fair comparisons.

For dataset, environment, configuration, or loading failures, continue to Troubleshooting.
path: Inspect results and diagnose a run

items.title: Run a hyperparameter sweep
items.text: Use a W&B sweep to search training configurations for an MSE or flow policy. Each trial runs the same trainer as an individual command. W&B chooses parameters; an agent on your machine launches the trials.

items.title: Before you run
items.text:
1. Complete setup and a small local training test.
  2. Authenticate using the W&B setup instructions.
  3. Work from hw1/ so configuration paths, data, and experiment outputs resolve correctly.

The supplied configurations launch real training and upload metrics and checkpoint artifacts. They use substantial training and evaluation budgets; they are not smoke tests. The YAML-to-CLI path is covered by automated tests with training mocked. No live sweep was run to validate this guide, and no runtime or score is promised.

items.title: 1. Choose and inspect a configuration
items.text:
File, relative to hw1/ Policy Additional search conf/sweeps/mse.yaml Direct action-chunk prediction Shared architecture and optimization parameters. conf/sweeps/flow.yaml Flow-based action-chunk prediction Also searches flow integration steps.

Read the configuration reference before changing a search space or budget. Both configurations maximize eval/mean_reward, whose W&B summary is configured to retain its maximum. Final evaluation uses separate random streams and is not the configured search objective.

items.title: 2. Register the sweep
items.text:
Run the command for the policy you chose:

hw1 · register an MSE sweep
uv run --no-sync wandb sweep conf/sweeps/mse.yaml
hw1 · register a flow sweep
uv run --no-sync wandb sweep conf/sweeps/flow.yaml

Registration contacts W&B and returns a sweep ID and URL; it does not launch training. Save the full ENTITY/PROJECT/SWEEP_ID printed by W&B. Registering both files creates separate sweeps with separate IDs. See the W&B registration documentation.

items.title: 3. Launch a bounded number of trials
items.text:
Replace the placeholder below with the full ID from registration:

hw1 · run up to five trials
uv run --no-sync python -m hw1_imitation.sweep_agent --count 5 ENTITY/PROJECT/SWEEP_ID

This starts real training on the machine running the agent. The count limits this agent invocation, not the entire sweep; the YAMLs do not set a sweep-wide run cap. Run one agent at a time initially to avoid competing for local compute.

The launcher accepts a positional sweep_id and optional --count; omitting the count leaves the agent without a local trial limit. It suppresses DEBUG and INFO messages from the parent W&B agent, including Running runs:, so routine status messages do not interrupt the training progress bar. Agent warnings and errors remain visible and can still interrupt the bar. The training subprocess's W&B startup messages, links, run history, and summary remain visible.

This launcher filters W&B's internal wandb.wandb_agent logger; it does not set WANDB_QUIET or WANDB_SILENT. Recheck that logger integration when upgrading W&B. The sweep YAML still launches hw1_imitation.train for each trial.

Each trial creates its own experiment directory under exp/, logs to W&B, and retains checkpoints. The supplied YAMLs disable videos but leave CSV logging and persistent checkpoint storage enabled through training defaults. See checkpoint behavior for retention and failure handling.

items.title: 4. Continue or change the search
items.text:
To request more trials for the same registered definition, reuse its ID:

hw1 · request five more trials
uv run --no-sync python -m hw1_imitation.sweep_agent --count 5 ENTITY/PROJECT/SWEEP_ID

Keep the code revision and environment recorded with the sweep. Reusing the ID does not restore your local code to its earlier state. If you change the local YAML, register a new sweep to use that definition; editing a file does not update the previously registered definition.

items.title: 5. Verify results before comparing trials
items.text:
1. Open the returned sweep URL and check trial status and sampled configuration.
  2. Inspect the maximum periodic evaluation reward alongside the full reward history.
  3. Confirm that a completed trial reports final/mean_reward and its selected checkpoint.
  4. Follow Inspect results for local artifacts and Compare experiments before declaring an improvement.

An objective value can exist before a trial completes. A failed or interrupted trial is not a completed final assessment. Confirm promising settings across multiple seeds instead of reporting only the strongest search result.

items.title: If the sweep fails
items.text:
Symptom Next check YAML file not found Run from hw1/ and use conf/sweeps/, not the former sweeps/ path. Authentication or project error Check W&B login, access to the project, and the full sweep ID. Trial rejects an argument Check the explicit-value CLI syntax and that the agent uses this checkout. Local YAML edits do not affect trials Register the changed definition and use its new ID. Final metrics are absent Inspect the trial process status and traceback; training or final evaluation may not have completed.

Continue to Troubleshooting for dataset, device, and checkpoint failures.

items.title: Save, load, and train further
items.text: Use a policy checkpoint to run inference, evaluate a saved policy, or initialize another training run. Complete setup and work from hw1/. Loading for inference does not need the original demonstration dataset.

items.title: Save the model and its normalization together
items.text:
The trainer saves at every selection evaluation. Persistent files use exp/<run>/checkpoints/policy_step_<step>.pt; see Inspect results to choose one.

When working directly with a policy and its matching normalizer, use the existing API:

from hw1_imitation.checkpoint import save_policy

# model and normalizer are an existing, matching pair.
save_policy("policy.pt", model, normalizer, flow_num_steps=10)

This writes a file and replaces an existing destination only after serialization succeeds. Keep model state stable during saving; do not have multiple writers target the same path. A policy file stores weights, architecture, normalization, dropout settings, and inference defaults. See the checkpoint contract for omissions and failure behavior.

items.title: Load for inference
items.text:
Provide an existing checkpoint and a NumPy batch of raw observations shaped (batch, model.state_dim). For this Push-T state interface, each observation contains the ordered five state values described in Push-T.

import torch
from hw1_imitation.checkpoint import load_policy
from hw1_imitation.randomness import RandomStreamFactory, StreamId

model, normalizer, inference = load_policy("policy.pt", device="cpu")
# raw_observations must be supplied from your compatible environment/data.
states = torch.as_tensor(
    normalizer.normalize_state(raw_observations), dtype=torch.float32,
)
streams = RandomStreamFactory(root_seed=42)
generator = streams.torch(StreamId.EVAL_POLICY, index=0, device=states.device)
with torch.no_grad():
    predicted = model.sample_actions(
        states, generator=generator, num_steps=inference["flow_num_steps"],
    )
actions = normalizer.denormalize_action(predicted.cpu().numpy())

Expected actions shape is (batch, model.chunk_size, model.action_dim) in raw action coordinates. The loader returns the model in evaluation mode. Clip to the environment's action bounds before stepping it; manual sampling above does not perform clipping.

Retain the generator across sequential predictions if you want its draws to advance. Recreating it with the same identity restarts the noise stream. For accelerator inference, move both the input tensor and generator to the model's device.

items.title: Evaluate in the supported environment
items.text:
For a compatible saved Push-T policy, this API call runs real environment episodes but does not train or download demonstrations:

from hw1_imitation.evaluation import evaluate_policy

result = evaluate_policy(
    model=model,
    normalizer=normalizer,
    device=next(model.parameters()).device,
    chunk_size=model.chunk_size,
    video_size=(256, 256),
    num_video_episodes=0,
    num_eval_episodes=10,
    flow_num_steps=inference["flow_num_steps"],
    streams=streams,
)
print(result.mean_reward, result.num_episodes)

This example assumes the model, normalizer, inference settings, and factory from the preceding snippet. It uses the evaluator's default selection streams. Ten episodes is an illustrative budget; record the budget and stream choices when comparing results. The evaluator handles normalization, action clipping, episode boundaries, and model-mode restoration.

items.title: Initialize another training run
items.text:
Replace the checkpoint path before running this real training command:

uv run --no-sync src/hw1_imitation/train.py \
  --init-from /path/to/policy.pt \
  --num-epochs 20 --lr 0.0001 \
  --log-wandb False --num-video-episodes 0 \
  --exp-name continued-policy

This starts a new 20-epoch run. It may download demonstrations and writes a new experiment directory, CSVs, and retained checkpoints. The command was source-checked, not executed for this guide.

State Behavior with --init-from Architecture, weights, normalizer Restored from the file. Fresh-model flags --policy-type, --hidden-dims, and --chunk-size do not replace them. Dropout probabilities Inherited per layer when --dropout-p is omitted; an explicit value overrides all layers. Use --dropout-p 0 to disable them. Flow evaluation steps Taken from the new invocation's --flow-num-steps or its default, not inherited by the trainer from the checkpoint. Optimizer, counters, root seed and generators Created fresh from the new invocation; no saved optimizer or RNG position exists. Data split, epoch budget, learning rate, monitoring Taken from the new invocation and its defaults. Logs and retention history Start in the new run.

A “fresh seed” means newly initialized streams from the selected seed, which may have the same integer value as before. It does not mean the trainer chooses a new random seed automatically.

items.title: Verify what was restored
items.text:
1. Confirm the startup summary reports loaded weights and the intended checkpoint.
  2. Check the effective architecture and horizon, especially if fresh-model flags were also supplied.
  3. Verify that new data has the same feature meanings, dimensions, and units; the saved normalizer is reused without refitting.
  4. Inspect the new run's outputs and final checkpoint selection using Inspect results.

Do not call this exact interrupted-run resumption: optimizer moments, RNG positions, and training position are absent. Do not bypass unsupported-version errors by loading legacy whole-model pickle files through another path. For deliberate format work, use Change the checkpoint format.

items.title: Early stopping
items.text: Plateau detection is independent of checkpoint selection and experiment tracking.

items.title: EarlyStopping dataclass
items.text:
EarlyStopping(patience: int, min_delta: float, start_step: int, objective: ObjectiveType, stale_steps: int = 0)

Request stopping after too many evaluations without sufficient improvement.

How it works

  • The first finite observation establishes a reference, even during warm-up.
  • An improvement must strictly exceed min_delta in the chosen direction. It replaces the reference and resets the stale-evaluation counter.
  • Otherwise, increment the counter only when step > start_step. Return True when the counter reaches patience.

Important behavior

  • Small gains can accumulate against the last reference, not the previous value.
  • Patience counts stale evaluations, not optimizer steps or epochs.
  • A stop signal is not latched: a later sufficient improvement clears it. The caller decides whether to exit the training loop.
  • Checkpoint selection is separate and can retain a better score even when its improvement is too small to reset patience.

See update for a worked example.

Attributes:

Name Type Description patience int

Positive number of stale evaluation updates needed to request stopping. This counts calls after warm-up, not elapsed optimizer steps or epochs.

min_delta float

Finite, nonnegative improvement threshold. A gain equal to this threshold does not reset patience, even when the threshold is zero.

start_step int

Nonnegative warm-up boundary in the caller's step units. Stale observations at or before this step do not increment the counter; sufficient improvements still update the reference.

objective ObjectiveType

Direction selected at construction: "min" for lower values or "max" for higher values. Reassigning this field does not rebuild the comparison function.

stale_steps int

Mutable stale-evaluation counter, initially zero unless supplied to the constructor. It is not validated or reset by initialization; a sufficient improvement resets it to zero.

reference_reward int

Reference observation for measuring improvement, despite the reward-specific name. Initialized to positive infinity for minimization or negative infinity for maximization, then replaced by each sufficiently improved finite observation.

_is_better int

Implementation detail: comparison callable selected during initialization. It reads the current reference_reward and min_delta when evaluating an observation.

items.title: __post_init__
items.text:
__post_init__() -> None

Validate settings and initialize the reference and comparison function.

Called automatically by the dataclass constructor.

  • Set the reference to positive infinity for "min", or negative infinity for "max".
  • Select the comparison direction from objective.
  • Leave stale_steps as supplied; this is not a full tracker reset.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If patience is nonpositive, start_step is negative, min_delta is nonfinite or negative, or objective is neither "min" nor "max".

Source code in hw1/src/hw1_imitation/early_stopping.py 
def __post_init__(self) -> None:
    """Validate settings and initialize the reference and comparison function.

    Called automatically by the dataclass constructor.

    - Set the reference to positive infinity for `"min"`, or negative
      infinity for `"max"`.
    - Select the comparison direction from `objective`.
    - Leave `stale_steps` as supplied; this is not a full tracker reset.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If `patience` is nonpositive, `start_step` is negative,
            `min_delta` is nonfinite or negative, or `objective` is neither
            `"min"` nor `"max"`.
    """
    if self.patience <= 0:
        raise ValueError("patience must be positive")
    if self.start_step < 0:
        raise ValueError("start_step must be nonnegative")
    if not math.isfinite(self.min_delta) or self.min_delta < 0:
        raise ValueError("min_delta must be finite and nonnegative")
    if self.objective not in ("min", "max"):
        raise ValueError(
            f"objective should be 'min' or 'max' but got {self.objective}"
        )

    # First initialization.
    self.reference_reward = np.inf if self.objective == "min" else -np.inf

    if self.objective == "min":
        self._is_better = lambda current: current < (
            self.reference_reward - self.min_delta
        )
    else:
        self._is_better = lambda current: current > (
            self.reference_reward + self.min_delta
        )

items.title: update
items.text:
update(value: float, step: int) -> bool

Record one evaluation and report whether patience is exhausted.

Apply the class's improvement and warm-up rules to mutate reference_reward and stale_steps. Reject nonfinite values before changing either field.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default value float

Finite observation to minimize or maximize. Compare against the stored reference using the strict min_delta threshold.

required step int

Progress coordinate used only for comparison with start_step. Training passes the optimizer step. No monotonicity or nonnegativity check is performed; repeated calls at the same eligible step each count as an evaluation.

required

Returns:

Name Type Description stop_requested bool

Whether the current stale_steps is at least patience. This signal is not latched: a later sufficient improvement resets the counter and returns False.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If value is NaN or either infinity.

Examples:

Warm up through step 10, then stop after two stale evaluations. A gain exactly equal to min_delta does not count as an improvement. The reference starts at 10, stays unchanged at 12, then advances to 13. Observations of 14 and 15 exhaust patience against that reference.

>>> tracker = EarlyStopping(2, 2.0, 10, objective="max")
>>> tracker.update(10.0, step=0)
False
>>> tracker.update(12.0, step=10)
False
>>> tracker.update(13.0, step=11)
False
>>> tracker.update(14.0, step=20)
False
>>> tracker.update(15.0, step=30)
True
Source code in hw1/src/hw1_imitation/early_stopping.py 
def update(self, value: float, step: int) -> bool:
    """Record one evaluation and report whether patience is exhausted.

    Apply the class's improvement and warm-up rules to mutate
    `reference_reward` and `stale_steps`. Reject nonfinite values before
    changing either field.

    Args:
        value: Finite observation to minimize or maximize. Compare against
            the stored reference using the strict `min_delta` threshold.
        step: Progress coordinate used only for comparison with `start_step`.
            Training passes the optimizer step. No monotonicity or
            nonnegativity check is performed; repeated calls at the same
            eligible step each count as an evaluation.

    Returns:
        stop_requested: Whether the current `stale_steps` is at least
            `patience`. This signal is not latched: a later sufficient
            improvement resets the counter and returns `False`.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If `value` is NaN or either infinity.

    Examples:
        Warm up through step 10, then stop after two stale evaluations. A gain
        exactly equal to `min_delta` does not count as an improvement. The
        reference starts at 10, stays unchanged at 12, then advances to 13.
        Observations of 14 and 15 exhaust patience against that reference.

        >>> tracker = EarlyStopping(2, 2.0, 10, objective="max")
        >>> tracker.update(10.0, step=0)
        False
        >>> tracker.update(12.0, step=10)
        False
        >>> tracker.update(13.0, step=11)
        False
        >>> tracker.update(14.0, step=20)
        False
        >>> tracker.update(15.0, step=30)
        True
    """
    if not math.isfinite(value):
        raise ValueError("Value tracked must be finite")

    if self._is_better(value):
        self.reference_reward = value
        self.stale_steps = 0
    else:
        if step > self.start_step:
            self.stale_steps += 1

    return self.stale_steps >= self.patience

BasePolicy(config: PolicyConfig)

Bases: Module

Define the shared interface for state-conditioned action-chunk policies.

Subclasses implement initialization, loss computation, and action sampling. Use the explicit methods rather than calling the policy as a module: this base class does not implement forward.

State and randomness

  • Architecture lives in config; learned parameters use the inherited PyTorch Module state interface.
  • Loss and sampling methods receive caller-owned generators. Active dropout and stochastic policy operations consume draws; deterministic paths do not.
  • The caller owns normalization, device placement, and train/eval mode.
